title: Session 1 — Participant 27 User + Claude Behavior Graphs
goal: GENERATE A REACH-BASED TERRAIN CROSS-SECTION ATLAS OF A DRAINAGE NETWORK AS A PRINT-READY PDF — TRANSECTS EVERY N METRES AT FIXED WIDTH, PROFILES TILED BY REACH, WITH FULL CARTOGRAPHIC APPARATUS — AND DELIVER A REPRODUCIBILITY PACKAGE (SURVEY FIELD BOOK, GPKG DATABASE, STYLE FILES, QGIS PROJECT TEMPLATE)
context:
Rivers and streams are usually studied not only from above, as lines on a map, but also in cross-section — imagine slicing the terrain perpendicular to the channel, like cutting a loaf of bread, and looking at the shape of each slice from the side. Each slice shows the channel bed, its banks, and how steeply the surrounding land rises away from the water. Engineers and risk analysts read these slices to understand how much water a channel can carry before it spills, where the floodplain is wide and flat, and which stretches are most exposed. My task is to produce these slices systematically along an entire drainage network — one every fixed distance, all the same width so they can be compared to each other — using a high-resolution terrain model built from airborne laser scanning.
The deliverable is an atlas: a multi-page PDF where each page covers one segment of the river, showing a map of that segment on top and its corresponding cross-sections below, together with the standard reference information any professional map must carry — coordinate system, scale, north arrow, a small locator map, and data attribution. Beyond the document itself, I also produce the underlying material that lets someone else regenerate or extend it: a spatial database of every cross-section, a tabular register of their coordinates and elevations, the styling files, and a working project file. The point is not just to make one PDF, but to build a repeatable process — which is why a later session will feed flood simulation results through the same machinery.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not:
The goal was partially achieved up to Step 5. Two hours of session time were not enough to complete the entire workflow. For this reason, Session 2 is proposed to resume the remaining steps, reorganizing them to meet the duration and complexity requirements.
Regarding the result of Step 5, it can be said that the objective of recreating the plate according to the requirements was achieved.

Step 1.step_name: Formalise the cartographic specification and QA criteria
Step 1.step_action: Hand Cowork the plotting rules and worked examples, plus quality criteria for map-window framing and profile distribution. Cowork converts them into an explicit, testable specification document and a machine-readable style token file that later steps consume.
Step 1.input: Profile plotting rules and example plates (images / prior deliverables); verbal QA criteria.
rubrics: Every rule I stated appears in the spec as a testable condition, not a paraphrase — each one can be checked against a finished plate with a yes/no answer.
All mandatory layout elements are enumerated with defined position and relative size: CRS, project name, attribution, location description, locator map, scale bar, north arrow.
style_tokens.json is valid, machine-readable, and covers colour, line weight, font and size for every layer and plot element referenced downstream.
Ambiguities in my instructions are surfaced as explicit questions or documented assumptions, not silently resolved.
Nothing appears in the spec that I did not ask for, unless clearly flagged as a suggestion for my approval.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The spec and style_tokens.json did what I asked: every plotting rule came back as a condition I can check against a finished plate with a yes/no answer, the mandatory layout block was fully enumerated, and the token file was valid and complete enough for Step 5 to consume without me editing it. The point I docked is that ambiguities in my instructions were resolved into documented assumptions rather than raised with me before drafting. The assumptions were written down and visible, so nothing was hidden — but I would have preferred to be asked first, because settling those choices upfront would have saved a review pass later. Rated 4 rather than 5 on that basis alone.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Both declared outputs were produced and both were usable downstream without rework: cartographic_spec.md became the reference I QA'd against in Step 5, and style_tokens.json was consumed directly by the plate composition code. Converting my verbal criteria into a testable written specification is exactly the task, and it was completed. What the agent did not do was reduce my own effort as much as I expected — I still carried the framing and the decisions, so the step felt more like dictation with good formatting than genuine offloading.

Step 2.step_action: Load the DTM, drainage network, orthomosaic and geomorphology layers. Cowork audits CRS agreement, raster resolution/nodata handling, extents/overlap, and drainage topology.
Step 2.output: Audit report; a corrected/filtered drainage layer if the topology needs repair.
Step 2.tools: Free: QGIS 3.x, Python (geopandas, rasterio). Paid: Claude Pro (Cowork).
rubrics: All four datasets are reported with CRS, extent, resolution or feature count, and nodata value — no dataset silently skipped.
CRS mismatches and any non-projected CRS are flagged for my decision, never silently reprojected.
Drainage topology problems are enumerated with counts and locations: dangles, disconnected segments, duplicate geometry, zero-length features.
DTM coverage is checked against the drainage extent, and nodata voids over channels are reported explicitly.
The audit is written to a file I can re-read later, not left only in the chat transcript.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The audit did what an audit is for: it caught the things that would have corrupted transect generation before I reached Step 3, rather than leaving me to discover them downstream. All four datasets — DTM, drainage network, orthomosaic, geomorphology — were reported with CRS, extent, resolution or feature count, and nodata value, with none silently skipped. CRS handling was correct in the way that matters most to me: mismatches were put in front of me as a decision instead of being reprojected quietly. Drainage topology was enumerated with counts and locations, so I could go straight to the offending features in QGIS, and DTM coverage was checked against the drainage extent with nodata voids over channels called out explicitly. The corrected drainage_clean layer was right and fed Step 3 without further repair. Rated 5 because the substance was complete; the one shortfall is about durability, not correctness.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The audit was thorough and correct, and the corrected drainage layer was produced and validated. This was the step where working with the agent clearly beat working alone: cross-checking CRS, resolution, nodata and topology across four heterogeneous datasets is exactly the kind of systematic, repetitive verification I would otherwise do by hand across several QGIS sessions. Nothing had to be re-explained, nothing had to be corrected, and the flagged issues were real issues.

Step 3.step_action: Propose a corrected drainage layer, then split the drainage network into named reaches and generate cross-section transects at every n metres along each reach, perpendicular to the local channel direction, all at identical width — the spatial-reasoning core of the session.
Step 3.input: Corrected drainage layer; n and transect width from the spec.
Step 3.output: reaches and transects layers (GPKG), with deterministic IDs.
Step 3.tools: Free: QGIS 3.x, Python (geopandas, shapely). Paid: Claude Pro (Cowork).
rubrics: Spacing along each reach matches n within tolerance, and every transect has exactly the specified width.
Transects are perpendicular to the local channel direction — verified visually in QGIS on meandering stretches, with no erratic orientations.
Confluences and reach endpoints are handled according to the spec rule; no transect unintentionally crosses two channels.
Overlapping or self-intersecting transects on tight meanders are detected and resolved as the spec dictates, rather than left in the output.
Transect and reach IDs are deterministic, reach-keyed, and stable across re-runs, so downstream steps do not break when Step 3 is repeated.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The final reaches and transects layers are correct and I would use them, but reaching that state took more iteration than any other step and this was one of the two overruns in the session. Spacing matched n within tolerance and every transect carried exactly the specified width. Confluences and reach endpoints followed the spec rule, with no transect unintentionally crossing two channels. Overlaps and self-intersections on tight meanders were detected and resolved as the spec dictates rather than left in the output. IDs were deterministic and reach-keyed, and stayed stable when I re-ran the step — which mattered, because I re-ran it. The shortfall was perpendicularity: on the first pass I found erratic transect orientations on meandering stretches when I checked visually in QGIS, and it took a correction round to get local channel direction handled properly. That check was mine, not the agent's, and it is the reason for a 4 rather than a 5. This is the step with the densest spatial reasoning, so I expected to iterate — but I would have preferred the agent to flag the meander cases itself.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The task was completed and the delivered geometry is sound — but it was completed collaboratively rather than autonomously, and that distinction is the honest description of this step. The agent understood the spatial rules I set out for confluences, meander handling and endpoint treatment, and when I came back with the orientation problem it diagnosed and fixed it without me having to specify the remedy. Deterministic, reach-keyed IDs held stable across re-runs, which is what made iterating cheap enough to be worth doing. The time saving was real but smaller than in the surrounding steps, because the correction round consumed much of it.

Step 4.step_name: Sample the DTM; build profile tables and survey field book
Step 4.step_action: Densify each transect, extract DTM elevation at every vertex, and assemble the per-transect profile series and survey field book, locking the naming convention Step 7's Atlas expression will need.
Step 4.tools: Free: QGIS 3.x, Python (rasterio, numpy, pandas). Paid: Claude Pro (Cowork).
rubrics: Elevation is sampled at the specified interval along every transect, with nodata represented explicitly rather than dropped or silently interpolated.
The survey field book has one row per transect carrying all required fields: ID, reach, station, start and end coordinates, azimuth, length, min/max/mean elevation.
Coordinates are written in the correct projected CRS at appropriate precision, with consistent column naming.
A spot check of three randomly chosen transects reproduces the same elevations I obtain by point-sampling the DTM directly in QGIS.
Profile record and file naming already follow the convention the Step 7 Atlas expression will require.

ratings.output_quality_reason: This step came out clean and I have no reservations about it. Elevation was sampled at the specified interval along every transect, with nodata represented explicitly rather than dropped or silently interpolated — which is the failure mode I was most concerned about, because interpolated voids over a channel would quietly corrupt every profile drawn from them. The survey field book has one row per transect carrying the full set of required fields: ID, reach, station, start and end coordinates, azimuth, length, and min/max/mean elevation. Coordinates are written in the correct projected CRS at appropriate precision with consistent column naming, so the CSV is directly usable as a field document rather than as an intermediate I would have to reformat. I spot-checked three randomly chosen transects by point-sampling the DTM directly in QGIS and the elevations matched. Profile record and file naming already follow the convention the Atlas expression will need in Session 2, so nothing has to be renamed later.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Every declared output was produced, correct on the first pass, and independently verified. This is the step where the agent contributed most relative to my own effort: bulk raster sampling along hundreds of densified transects and assembling the results into a correctly typed, correctly projected table is precise, repetitive work that is slow and error-prone by hand, and it came back right without correction rounds. Getting the naming convention aligned to a Session 2 requirement at this stage — rather than discovering the mismatch when building the Atlas expression — is the kind of forward-looking consistency that saves an entire rework pass.

All profiles share the same x-extent, and the agreed vertical exaggeration policy is applied identically across every plate.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The reference plate is the plate I specified, and I would sign it off as the design for the atlas. Every mandatory layout element is present and genuinely populated — CRS, project name, attribution, location description, inset locator map, scale bar and north arrow are all real content, with no placeholder text and no empty locator. The profiles share a common x-extent and the agreed vertical exaggeration policy is applied as specified, so plates generated from this function will stay comparable to one another. Map window framing follows the spec: the reach is fully contained, the zoom rule is the one I asked for, and the transect lines read clearly over the orthomosaic. I checked the scale bar against true ground distance and confirmed the north arrow reflects the actual projection rather than being decorative. The one thing not demonstrated is the print-ready PDF: the output was rendered as PNG, so page-size behaviour, text overlap and label legibility at 100% in the final print format are not yet proven. Since the objective of this step as it actually ran was to prove the design and I consider the design proven, I rate the output 5 and note the PDF gap separately.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The step produced a reusable plate composition function taking a reach_id, and a rendered reference plate that meets the Step 1 criteria — which is what the step needed to deliver for the atlas build to proceed. Getting there took correction rounds on the rendering, and translating cartographic intent into a layout the agent framed correctly required more back-and-forth than the earlier steps, which is why I marked understanding at 4: composition judgement is harder to communicate in words than a geoprocessing rule. Once corrected, the agent adapted precisely and I never lost control of the design decisions. Composing a full cartographic plate programmatically — map window, tiled profile grid, and the complete complementary block — is substantial work that would have taken me considerably longer alone, so the effort saving was real even with the iteration.
